projects.cardDescription: Tested whether complaint themes inside Steam reviews rise before a game's review score collapses. They don't — both events were triggered by dated developer announcements, so themes and score moved the same day. The useful finding is same-day diagnosis: the theme mix names the cause within hours.
projects.impactStat: A 12-point single-day drop rule fires 3 times in 9 months with zero false alarms; the obvious level rule fires 35 times, 29 of them nothing
projects.oneSentenceDescription: 886,850 Steam reviews across a launch, a review-bomb and a balance controversy, testing whether complaint themes give early warning of a score collapse — and finding they don't.
projects.targetIndustryRole: Gaming / community and live-ops teams monitoring launch sentiment
projects.summaryImpact:
**The question was whether complaint themes lead the review score.** If crash complaints spike three days before the score moves, a community team has a usable early-warning signal. I tested it on HELLDIVERS 2 — 886,850 Steam reviews across 271 days covering the launch, the PSN account-linking review-bomb, and the August balance controversy.

**They don't lead.** Both sentiment collapses were triggered by dated developer actions, so complaints and the score moved on the same day. On 2024-05-02 the game sat at 86.7% positive on 968 reviews; the next day Sony announced PSN account linking and the day carried 36,055 reviews at 62.8%, with Sony/PSN complaints going from 21% to 57%. You cannot get early warning of an announcement from reactions to it.

**What the data does support is same-day diagnosis.** The theme mix names the cause within hours, in both directions — Sony/PSN up in May while balance complaints fell; balance 0% to 46% in August while Sony/PSN stayed flat. That is a real operational tool, just not the one I set out to build.
projects.problemSpace:
When a live game's review score falls, the community team's first two questions are what is this about and did we miss a warning sign. The second question is the valuable one: a theme that reliably spikes before the aggregate moves would let a team get ahead of a story instead of reacting to it.

HELLDIVERS 2 is a good test case because it launched well and soured later, which leaves a genuine positive baseline to measure a change against. A game that launched badly gives you nothing to compare to. It also contains two structurally different events: a policy announcement that triggered one of the largest review-bombs in Steam's history, and a balance patch that produced a deeper sentiment trough at a fiftieth of the volume.

stakeholders.description: Needs to know what a spike is about before writing a response, and whether it is still getting worse.
Needs to separate a policy problem from a balance problem from a stability problem, because the fixes sit with different teams.
Wants an early-warning metric. The honest answer here is that review text cannot provide one.

inputs.description: Every public Steam review for HELLDIVERS 2 between 2024-02-08 and 2024-11-04 — 886,850 of them, pulled from Valve's public appreviews endpoint. No API key, no sampling. Sentiment is Steam's own thumbs-up flag rather than a text model, for reasons in Execution.

stats.label: official patches, from the developer's own announcements

dataQuality.label: What the corpus is and isn't
items: **Self-selected.** Steam reviewers are people moved enough to write, not players. Both events here were the kind that motivate writing.
**The thumbs-up is binary.** Of 200 hand-labelled reviews, 19 were genuinely mixed — 'great game, terrible servers' counts identically to 'perfect'. Ambivalence is understated throughout.

**Theme analysis is English-only**, dropping roughly a quarter of the corpus. The largest excluded group is Simplified Chinese, whose complaints may differ on exactly the regional-access issue one event was about.

**Reddit was never pulled** — a scope decision, not a coverage finding. It also removes the likeliest place a lead could have appeared, since complaints usually surface in discussion before they surface as reviews.

closingNote.label: Coverage was verified, not assumed
items: Every chunk of the pull is checked against Steam's own count for that date range and retried if short. Final coverage 100.0%, zero duplicate IDs, zero out-of-window items.
This check exists because the first version did not have it — see Discovery.

surprisingPatterns.label: Surprising Pattern
items: **The review-bomb week was the least duplicated week in the corpus** — 20.7% repeated text against a 28-30% baseline. I expected mass-pasted copypasta to inflate it. Instead the most-repeated texts were positive community memes ('for democracy', 11,851 times), and the only clearly coordinated negative repeats were 'sony' and 'psn' at 0.8% of the week. The collapse was overwhelmingly people writing their own words.

**The famous event was not the deepest one.** The PSN review-bomb produced 76,741 reviews in a day. The August balance patch produced a lower positive share (53.7% on 2024-08-07) at roughly a fiftieth of the volume. Loudest and worst are different measurements.

hypothesisVsReality.label: Hypothesis vs. Reality
items: **Expected:** complaint themes rise days before the aggregate score moves. **Found:** nothing leads. Raw cross-correlation suggested leads in seven of eight themes, up to 12 days — all of it dissolved under three robustness checks.

**Expected:** a sentiment model would be needed to read the reviews. **Found:** two standard models both scored worse than guessing the majority class, and Steam's own thumbs-up flag matched my hand labels far better than either.

**Expected:** review-bomb copypasta would distort the picture and need down-weighting. **Found:** collapsing every repeated text to a single vote changes the headline gap by 0.7 percentage points. The decision did not matter.

deadEnds.label: What didn't work
items: **The first full pull returned 65,496 of 858,566 reviews — 7.6% — with no error.** Steam's cursor pagination stops serving at around 650 pages on a wide date range and simply ends. February through April were missing entirely. Fixed by bisecting the window on Steam's own review counts until every chunk paginates shallowly.

**My integrity check passed that truncated pull.** Duplicate IDs, window bounds, empty text, timestamp gaps — all clean, because every review collected *was* genuine. There were just 92% too few. A validation that only inspects the rows present cannot detect the rows absent, and comparing against an independent total is now the first check rather than an afterthought.

**The cache faithfully preserved the bug.** A bad response was written to disk like any other, so re-running replayed the truncation exactly. Retries had to be made to bypass the cache before they did anything.

**The six-month window truncated the one event worth testing.** The August controversy began three days before the window closed. I extended to 271 days, because a null measured on a truncated event is an artefact of the window rather than a result.

executionDeadEnds.label: The result I nearly published
items: Raw cross-correlation produced a clean-looking table showing a 12-day lead for developer-conduct complaints. It was noise. Reporting the best of 29 lags means taking the extreme of 29 attempts, and chance alone produces a median best-of-29-lags correlation of about −0.15 — most of what the table showed.

A rotation test, a correction for testing eight themes, and a sensitivity check on how thin a day is allowed to be each removed it independently. The apparent leads moved from +3 to +12 to −8 days as measurement improved, which is what noise does and a real signal does not.

methodology.heading: Pull, verified against an independent count
methodology.description: Cursor-paginated pull of Valve's public appreviews endpoint, chunked by bisecting on Steam's own review counts so no single query paginates deep enough to truncate. Every page cached by (appid, cursor, date range); every chunk checked against the expected count and retried with the cache bypassed if short.

methodology.heading: Sentiment: Steam's flag, after rejecting two models
methodology.description: I hand-labelled 200 reviews blind and tested both scorers against them. **VADER agreed 61.5%, a RoBERTa sentiment model 64.0% — against a 72.0% majority-class baseline.** Both did worse than always guessing 'positive'. The failure is specific: this game's players express enthusiasm through violence and self-deprecation ('I got hit by an explosion, shot into the air, then stomped by a robot 10/10'), which general-purpose models read as negative. Steam's own thumbs-up matched my labels 95.0%, so the index uses that and the models stay in the repo as the evidence for the decision.

methodology.heading: Themes: a keyword taxonomy, seeded from the data
methodology.description: Nine themes, 182 seed phrases, mined by measuring which terms are distinctive of thumbs-down reviews rather than guessed. Matching is word-boundary substring — transparent and explainable line by line, which a learned classifier would not be. Multi-label, because 'nerfed into the ground and it crashes' is genuinely two complaints. Coverage 69.6%; the remainder is partly missing vocabulary and partly complaint with no complaint words in it.

methodology.heading: The lag test, and why composition not volume
methodology.description: Themes are measured as a share of each day's negatives, not as raw counts. Volume and the aggregate score are both functions of how many people were angry that day, so correlating them recovers a relationship that exists by construction. Both series are differenced before correlating, because levels are dominated by one enormous event.

methodology.heading: Three checks before believing the result
methodology.description: A rotation-based permutation test built for the statistic actually reported (best of 29 lags); a Bonferroni correction for testing eight themes; and a sensitivity sweep on minimum day size. A test in the suite plants a three-day lead in synthetic data and asserts the method recovers it — reporting a null is only honest if the method could have found a signal.

methodology.heading: The threshold, derived rather than asserted
methodology.description: Candidate alert rules were tested against the data. A level rule ('below 72% positive') fires on 35 of 271 days, 29 of them nothing. A 12-point single-day drop fires three times in nine months — 3 May, 6 and 7 August — with no false alarms. At 10 points it adds four non-events; at 20 it misses August entirely.

keyResults.label: Key Results
items: **No theme leads the score.** Only Sony/PSN complaints correlate with it at all (r = −0.30), and the best lag is zero. Every apparent lead failed at least one of three robustness checks.
**Same-day diagnosis works.** On 2024-05-03 Sony/PSN complaints went 21% to 57% while balance complaints fell; on 2024-08-06 balance went 0% to 46% while Sony/PSN stayed at 3%.
**A change-based alert beats a level-based one decisively.** 3 alerts with zero false positives, against 35 alerts with 29 false positives for the obvious threshold.
**Recovery is as visible as collapse.** 2024-05-06 — the day Sony reversed — was the busiest day in the corpus at 78,185 reviews and 88.3% positive, up from 67.9% the day before.

projects.businessInterpretation:
For a community team, this is an instrumentation tool rather than a forecast. It will not tell you a storm is coming, because in both of these cases the storm was the studio's own announcement on a date it chose. What it will do is answer 'what is this about' within hours of a score moving, without anyone reading a review — and it distinguishes a policy problem from a balance problem from a stability problem, which matters because those fixes sit with three different teams.

On the headline being a null: this is a good outcome, better than forcing a fake finding. The first correlation table showed a twelve-day lead and looked publishable; three checks later there was nothing there.

The alerting recommendation is the practical output: watch the day-over-day change, not the level. A level threshold fires on a quarter of the calendar and a team learns to ignore it inside a fortnight. If genuine early warning is the goal, it needs data that moves before the announcement — crash telemetry, refund rates, or discussion-thread volume — none of which lives in review text.

items.text: Alert on a 12-point single-day fall in positive share, not on the level. When it trips, read the theme mix before reading reviews — it named the cause correctly in both events here, within hours.
Expect no warning from review text for announcement-driven events. The gap between a decision landing and sentiment moving was under 24 hours both times.

The headline here is a null, and the interesting work is in what it took to trust it: a truncated pull that looked clean, an integrity check that passed it, and a 12-day 'lead' that three independent checks dissolved.

limitations: Steam reviewers self-select — this measures people moved enough to write, not players.
Sentiment is Steam's binary thumbs-up. 19 of 200 hand-labelled reviews were genuinely mixed and the flag cannot represent them, so ambivalence is understated throughout.

Theme matching is keyword-based at 69.6% coverage. Some of the remainder is unreachable by any keyword list — 'Arrowhead struck gold but are determined to find copper' is a complaint with no complaint vocabulary in it.
Theme analysis is English-only, excluding roughly a quarter of the corpus — most notably Simplified Chinese reviews, on a project where one of the two events was about regional access.
Two events in one game. The mechanism (announcement-driven events cannot be predicted from reactions) should generalise; the specific thresholds should not be assumed to.
nextSteps: Test the same method on a launch whose sentiment decayed gradually rather than breaking on an announcement — that is where a lead could plausibly exist.
Add discussion-forum or Reddit volume as a second source, since complaints usually surface there before they surface as reviews.
Topic modelling as a cross-check on the ~30% of complaints no keyword reaches.

visuals.caption: Both collapses land on a dated developer action. The score recovers within days of the PSN reversal; the August trough is deeper but far smaller in volume.

projects.title: F2P vs Paid: Pricing and Engagement on Steam
projects.cardDescription: Does going free-to-play actually buy engagement? Across 20,761 Steam games, free titles are played a quarter as long as paid ones — and comparing within genre makes the gap wider, not narrower.
projects.impactStat: Free games are played a quarter as long as paid ones — 124 median minutes against 530 — and correcting for genre widens the gap rather than explaining it
projects.oneSentenceDescription: A 20,761-game study of whether going free-to-play actually buys engagement on Steam, built to kill the tautology that free things get downloaded more, and to test whether any gap survives comparing like genre with like.
projects.targetIndustryRole: Data Analyst, Data Scientist (gaming, product analytics)

sectionHeadlines.summaryImpact: Going free does not buy engagement
sectionHeadlines.problemSpace: More owners is a tautology, not a finding
sectionHeadlines.inputs: 26,017 apps, and a metric rebuilt mid-project
sectionHeadlines.discovery: The headline metric had no data behind it
sectionHeadlines.execution: The correction meant to explain the gap widened it
sectionHeadlines.results: Price predicts engagement better than the pricing model

summaryMetrics.label: genres holding enough of both models to compare within
tests across the pull, the cohort and the statistics

projects.summaryImpact: I set out to test a claim studios act on: that going free-to-play buys engagement. On Steam it does not. Across 20,761 games released since 2015, free games have a median playtime of 124 minutes against 530 for paid ones — a gap of more than four to one. The obvious objection is that free games cluster in genres that are simply played less, so I compared within genre across the 58 genres holding enough of both models. That correction was supposed to shrink the gap. It widened it, from a Cliff's delta of -0.457 to -0.482. The finding is not that the free-to-play advantage is a genre effect. It is that there is no advantage to explain.
projects.problemSpace: A studio choosing a launch pricing model, or a publisher weighing whether to take an ageing paid title free, wants to know what the model buys in engagement. The trap is that the obvious analysis answers a different question: free games have more owners, which is a tautology, because free things get downloaded. The question worth asking is whether players who take a free game stay in it as long as players who paid, and whether any difference holds once you stop comparing a free MOBA against a paid visual novel.

stakeholders.description: Choosing a launch pricing model, where the engagement consequence is usually assumed rather than measured.
Weighing a free-to-play conversion for an existing paid title.
Forecasting engagement from price, and sizing what a free launch will and will not deliver.

inputs.description: SteamSpy's full catalogue, enriched app by app from the Steam storefront for AUD price, genres, release date and the free-to-play flag. Playtime comes from Steam review payloads — real per-player figures, sampled at up to 200 reviewers per game. Every response is cached to disk untransformed, so a re-run returns identical data and an interrupted pull resumes rather than restarting.

dataQuality.label: What the data will not tell you
items: Ownership is a band, never a number — SteamSpy reports "1,000,000 .. 2,000,000" because Steam's privacy changes ended exact counts. It is carried as an interval throughout, and every owner-dependent result is recomputed at the lower bound, the midpoint and the upper bound.

5,256 apps were excluded and counted rather than quietly dropped: 3,052 released before 2015, 1,790 with no usable price, 261 that are software rather than games, and 153 with no parseable release date.
Both sources report current state, not launch state, so a paid game that went free years ago reads as free today.
The owner floor excludes games that flopped, which tilts the sample toward titles that found an audience.

closingNote.label: Reproducibility
items: 105 tests cover the pull, the cohort construction, the interval handling and the statistics — including the rank test, which is implemented directly rather than imported.

categoryLeader.label: Where engagement actually concentrates
categoryLeader.heading: Paid games at 60 AUD and above
categoryLeader.description: Median playtime rises monotonically across every price band — 233 minutes under 10 AUD, 630 in 10-30, 1,420 in 30-60, and 2,484 above 60. This is the strongest signal in the study, and it is not a claim that price causes engagement: price is standing in for production budget, scope and buyer intent, none of which this data measures.

surprisingPatterns.label: Where free-to-play does win
items: Free-to-play wins in exactly one genre — **Clicker**, 530 minutes against 218 — and ties in **Idler** (2,723 against 1,764). Both are built around long, low-intensity sessions, and in both the free model is native rather than a discount.

**MMORPG is the informative loss.** It is the genre where a free model should have its strongest case — persistent worlds, long tails, monetisation designed in — and paid titles still hold more than twice the playtime (2,810 against 1,216).
The losses elsewhere are heavy and consistent: Racing -0.827, Visual Novel -0.726, Point & Click -0.600.

hypothesisVsReality.label: What I expected, and what happened
items: **Expected:** that the naive gap was largely a genre artefact — free-to-play concentrates in genres that play short, and correcting for genre would collapse the difference.
**Found:** the genre-adjusted effect size (-0.482) is slightly *larger* than the naive one (-0.457). Whatever produces the gap, it is not the mix of genres that go free.
That is the more useful result. A confirmation would have explained the gap away; this says the gap is real inside genres too.

deadEnds.label: The headline metric died mid-project
items: The plan was to use SteamSpy's median playtime. It still serves the field — as zeroes. All four playtime fields return zero for every one of the 1,000 apps on the first catalogue page, and for both apps I spot-checked by hand.
The plain reading is that Steam's profile-privacy changes removed the sample those figures were derived from, leaving the old schema in place. Every playtime option the plan offered died at once.

Rebuilt on per-player playtime from Steam review payloads, which are populated. That buys real data at the cost of a smaller sample and a second selection bias — reviewers play more than owners do — both stated rather than absorbed.

methodology.heading: Rank-based comparison
methodology.description: Playtime is severely skewed — a handful of thousand-hour players drag any mean off the map — so every comparison uses Mann-Whitney U with tie and continuity corrections, and Cliff's delta as the effect size. Delta reads directly: -1 means every paid game outplays every free one, 0 means no separation.

methodology.heading: Effect size leads, p-value follows
methodology.description: At this sample size almost anything is statistically significant, so significance says little about magnitude. An effect size shown next to a visible cell count claims less and means more.

methodology.heading: Genre from user tags, not store genres
methodology.description: Steam's storefront genres are three broad buckets — ELDEN RING is simply "Action, RPG". The confound this study corrects for lives at the level of MOBA against Souls-like, which only the tags capture.

methodology.heading: Stratified pooling
methodology.description: Within-genre results are pooled by pairwise weight, and only across cells holding at least eight games of each model. A stratified estimate built from cells too thin to read individually would launder the same noise.

methodology.heading: Interval-aware ownership
methodology.description: Inclusion is released 2015 or later with an owner-interval midpoint above 20,000 — a threshold aligned to SteamSpy's own bottom band rather than chosen freehand. Every owner-dependent result is recomputed at all three bounds.

secondaryModel.label: A second metric, as a cross-check
items: Concurrent players per owner, computed across the whole 20,761-game cohort rather than the playtime sample. It agrees on direction (naive -0.109, genre-adjusted -0.092) and independently reproduces the price-band gradient.

It cannot carry the headline, and the reason is worth stating: 54% of the cohort has a concurrent-player count of exactly zero, so a rank test on it is mostly ties. It was also rejected as the headline metric on a measurement argument — it penalises single-player paid games structurally, which sits too close to the variable under test.

executionDeadEnds.label: Two approaches tried and rejected
items: **Ranking genre tags by vote count.** Dota 2's highest-voted tag is "Free to Play" at 60,040 votes, three times the next. That rule would have sorted every free game into a "Free to Play" stratum and left no cell containing both models — the strata would have restated the variable under test. Business-model tags are now excluded by name.

**Using the highest-voted eligible tag.** Steam's umbrella tags outrank the informative ones on most games, so this put 65% of the cohort into buckets like "Action" or "Casual" — no better than the store genres the tags were meant to replace. Specific tags now beat umbrellas regardless of votes, which brought that to 18%.

keyResults.label: What the numbers say
items: **Free-to-play median playtime 124 minutes against 530 for paid**, across 1,198 free and 1,599 paid games with a usable reviewer sample.
Cliff's delta **-0.457 naive, -0.482 after genre adjustment** across 58 genres. The correction moved the result 0.025 further from zero, not toward it.

The three owner bounds agree to within 0.001. The interval assumption is the most visible judgement call in the study, and it does not drive the conclusion — because the comparisons are rank-based, widening or narrowing the bands barely reorders anything.
Among paid games, median playtime rises monotonically with price: 233 minutes under 10 AUD, 630 in 10-30, 1,420 in 30-60, 2,484 above 60.

projects.businessInterpretation: Going free does not buy engagement on Steam, and the genre mix does not explain the shortfall. The two genres where free-to-play holds its own, Clicker and Idler, are designed around long low-intensity sessions, which suggests the model works where the game's loop already suits it rather than as a general lever. Price level is the stronger predictor, climbing more than tenfold from the cheapest band to the most expensive — though the honest causal reading is that expensive games are not engaging because they are expensive. Price is standing in for production budget, scope and buyer intent, none of which this data measures.

items.text: Treat a free-to-play launch as a distribution decision, not an engagement one. It buys reach, and this data gives no reason to expect it to buy time played.

Check the genre's session structure before assuming the model transfers. Free-to-play held its own only in loops built for long passive play — Clicker and Idler — and lost everywhere else, including MMORPG.
Pair this with revenue per player before making a pricing call. Engagement is half the question, and the half this data cannot answer: a game played half as long may still earn more per player.

limitations: A median over reviewers is not a median over owners. People who write reviews have played more than people who don't, so every playtime figure here is biased upward. It stays comparable across games, which is what the question needs, but it is not an estimate of what a typical owner played.

Attrition is uneven. 700 of the 3,497 sampled games had fewer than 30 reviewers and were dropped rather than given a median on thin evidence — 22.5% of paid games against 16.5% of free ones. The paid sample therefore lost more of its small titles, and small titles plausibly play shorter, so the gap is more likely overstated than understated.
Current state is not launch state, so this cannot say what a conversion does to a specific title. That needs a before-and-after on the same game.
There is no revenue data here at all. Engagement is not monetisation.
nextSteps: Pair the engagement figures with revenue per player to answer the pricing question properly.
Run a before-and-after on titles that actually converted from paid to free, which is the only way to isolate the model from the game.
Extend the genre vocabulary using the coverage audit's ranked list of unclassified tags, and re-run to see whether any within-genre result moves.

projects.cardDescription: A Windows prototype for people who find fast or multi-part spoken questions hard to follow. It captures desktop audio, transcribes it, splits the question into parts and drafts three editable replies. Nothing is sent or spoken for the user.

projects.oneSentenceDescription: A personal prototype, built in August 2026, that turns a spoken question heard through a PC's speakers into a plain-language breakdown and three reply drafts the user can edit, ignore or replace.
projects.summaryImpact:
In a meeting, a question can arrive fast and in three parts while you're still working out the first. For people who process speech more slowly, lose track of multi-part questions, or find it hard to put an answer into words under time pressure, the difficulty isn't hearing the words. It's the gap between hearing a question and replying to it.

ConverseAssist is a personal prototype I made in August 2026 to explore that gap. It listens to the audio playing on a Windows PC, such as a video call, and transcribes it. It then works out whether a reply is likely needed, breaks the question into numbered parts, and drafts three replies: short, detailed, and a request to clarify. Every suggestion is editable and optional. The app never sends, posts or speaks a reply on the user's behalf.

Under the hood, a small C#/.NET 9 helper captures desktop audio through Windows WASAPI. A Node.js server sends the audio to a speech-to-text model, then sends the transcript to a language model constrained to a strict JSON schema. A plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript interface shows the result.

**How I built it:** I came up with the idea, designed the features and interface, and wrote pseudocode for each part. I refined the design with ChatGPT and used it as a coding assistant to turn that pseudocode into working code.

**It's a prototype.** It runs on one Windows machine and sends conversation audio to an external AI provider. I've used it in several real conversations, but nobody else has tested it yet.

projects.problemSpace:
Live captions solve part of the problem: they show what was said. They don't help with what comes next. That means working out what's actually being asked, keeping every part of a long question in mind, and finding words for an answer before the pause gets awkward.

The design brief I worked from set a few rules early. The tool supports the person; it doesn't speak for them. It should only offer answers when a reply is likely needed, always include a way to ask for clarification or more time, and never invent the user's opinions or experiences. Listening status must be obvious, with an immediate way to stop.

It isn't built around one diagnosis. The brief describes people who may find it difficult to process speech quickly, follow multi-part questions or respond under time pressure, for reasons that vary from person to person.

stakeholders.description: Needs the question broken down and a starting point for a reply, without losing control of what they actually say.
Their speech is captured and sent to an AI service, so their consent and any meeting or workplace rules matter.
Would need privacy, security, accessibility and legal review before anyone relied on it. None of that has happened yet.

inputs.description:
The app works with three kinds of input.

**Desktop audio:** everything playing through the PC's default output device, captured through Windows WASAPI loopback. It doesn't capture the microphone, so the user's own voice isn't recorded.

**An uploaded recording:** a common audio format up to 20 MB, for testing with prerecorded conversations.

**A built-in fictional example:** a sample question from a made-up colleague, so the interface can be tried without an API key or real audio.

Users can also save their preferred tone and reply length, phrases to use or avoid, and answers to questions they hear often.

dataQuality.label: What stays on the computer, and what doesn't
items: **Stays local:** the audio capture itself; the temporary WAV file, which is deleted once it's processed or discarded; saved answers and preferences, kept in a local file excluded from version control and in the browser's storage; and the end-of-session summary, which the browser assembles from earlier results. The local server only accepts connections from the same machine, and the API key never reaches the browser.

**Sent to an external AI provider:** the recorded audio, for transcription; the transcript, or the user's corrected version of it; the user's reply preferences and up to three saved answers the app picked as most relevant; and any draft the user asks to rewrite. The provider is Groq in the current configuration, and the code can be pointed at OpenAI instead.
**Not private by default.** Conversation audio leaves the machine whenever real processing runs. A mock mode and the built-in example send nothing, but they don't process real speech.

hypothesisVsReality.label: Planned vs. built
items: **Planned:** start with prerecorded audio files and leave live audio for a later phase. **Built:** both. File upload works, and live desktop-audio capture was added as a second-phase experiment. It processes the conversation in segments rather than as word-by-word live captions.

**Planned:** a React/TypeScript front end, a Python/FastAPI backend and Azure AI Speech. **Built:** a dependency-free Node.js server, plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript, a small C# helper for audio, and OpenAI-compatible APIs (Groq by default).

**Planned, not built:** Microsoft Teams or Graph integration, a rolling context window across the conversation, speaker identification from the audio, and testing with target users. The app guesses the speaker's name from the transcript text only.

methodology.heading: 1. Capture, only after the user confirms
methodology.description: Listening can't start until the user ticks a consent box. A C# helper opens the default output device in WASAPI loopback mode, writes a WAV file and reports the audio level. The interface shows a visible listening status, an elapsed-time counter and a level meter. **Manual mode** records until the user presses Stop. **Automatic mode** ends a segment after 1.8 seconds of silence following speech, or at 45 seconds, processes it, then starts listening again. Segments with no speech are discarded without being sent.

methodology.heading: 2. Transcribe, and let the user fix it
methodology.description: The Node.js server sends the recording to a speech-to-text model (Whisper large-v3-turbo through Groq in the current configuration). Transcripts can be wrong, so the user can correct the text and re-run the analysis on their correction rather than on what the model misheard.

methodology.heading: 3. Break the question down and draft replies
methodology.description: The transcript goes to a language model with written constraints and a strict JSON schema. The instructions tell it to simplify only what was said, never invent the user's views or experiences, leave `[add ...]` placeholders where personal details are missing, lower its confidence when unsure, and always include a clarification option. The schema fixes the shape of the answer: whether a reply is likely needed, up to five question parts, three drafts, a confidence level, and notes on names, decisions, actions and unanswered questions. The browser checks the result again before showing it.

methodology.heading: 4. Review, edit, choose
methodology.description: The interface shows the transcript, a plain-language breakdown of what's being asked, and the three drafts in tabs. The user can edit a draft, ask for it shorter, simpler, friendlier, more professional or as bullet points, swap in a support phrase such as asking for a moment to think, copy it, or have it read aloud. Nothing is sent anywhere automatically.

methodology.heading: Personalisation and saved answers
methodology.description: Users can set tone, length, a plain-language preference, and phrases to use or avoid. They can also store answers to questions they hear often, with key points each suggestion must include. Before each request, the app scores saved answers against the transcript by shared keywords and sends only the three best matches. When the model builds on a saved answer, the interface labels it. A private practice mode lets users rehearse saved answers against a timer and check which key points they covered.

methodology.heading: Accessibility controls
methodology.description: Larger text, a high-contrast mode, a reduced-distraction mode that hides helper text, and a focus mode that hides settings and secondary panels. Listening, processing, error and result messages are announced through screen-reader live regions. Reply tabs support arrow-key navigation, and there's a skip link, visible focus outlines and reduced-motion support. Keyboard shortcuts cover copying a reply, switching drafts and starting or stopping listening. A compact pop-up window can sit beside a video call.

executionDeadEnds.label: Technical challenges
items: **A web page can't record system audio by itself.** Capturing what the speakers are playing needs Windows audio APIs, so a separate C# console helper does the capture through WASAPI's COM interfaces. It talks to the Node.js server over plain text lines (`READY`, `LEVEL` and a stop command), which keeps both sides simple.

**Knowing when someone has finished asking.** Automatic mode uses a basic silence rule on the audio level, not speech detection. It's easy to reason about, but a long pause mid-question can split it in two, and steady background sound can hold a segment open until the 45-second cap.

**Model output the interface can rely on.** Free text would be hard to lay out consistently, so replies are forced into a strict schema with fixed fields and allowed values. Output that doesn't match is rejected with an error rather than shown half-formed.

**Useful suggestions vs. sending personal data.** Sending every saved answer would give the model more to work with, and send more personal information. Local keyword matching narrows it to three. It matches words, not meaning, so a reworded question can miss the right saved answer.

keyResults.label: Testing: what has and hasn't been checked
items: **Automated tests: 8 of 8 passing**, using Node's built-in test runner, re-run on 21 September 2026. They cover the three reply types, the fallback when an unknown draft is requested, audio-file validation, the strict output schema, limits on saved answers, saved-answer matching, the server refusing to analyse before a recording exists, and the local server serving only the page's own files, never the API key or saved answers.
**Build check:** the C# capture helper compiles with no warnings.
**Not covered by automated tests:** real audio capture, live transcription, the language-model call and the interface itself. They depend on audio hardware, an API key and a browser.

**My own use:** I've used it in several informal conversations, with the other person's knowledge, and it worked end to end: capture, transcript, question breakdown and reply drafts. That's hands-on use by the person who designed it, not a user study, and nothing was measured.

**No testing with other users and no accessibility audit.** Nobody but me has tried it, and it hasn't been evaluated against WCAG. The accessibility features above are design choices, not measured outcomes.

projects.businessInterpretation:
The prototype shows the whole chain working on one machine: Windows audio capture, speech-to-text, a constrained language-model call, and an interface designed around accessibility and user control rather than automation.

My own use shows it can keep up with a real conversation. It doesn't show that it helps other people. Does breaking a question into parts actually ease the pressure of replying? Are three drafts useful, or just more to read? Is segment-by-segment processing fast enough for a real conversation? Only testing with the intended users can answer those.

items.text: Get consent from everyone whose speech is captured, check meeting and workplace policies, and complete a security and privacy review. The in-app consent box is the user confirming for themselves. It can't collect anyone else's consent.
Try it with a small group from the intended audience, using realistic fictional conversations, and find out whether it helps before adding features.
Run a proper evaluation with screen readers, keyboard-only use and WCAG checks, rather than relying on the features being present.

limitations: Windows only, on one machine, started from a terminal. There's no installer and no hosted version.
Processing is per segment, not live captioning. The user waits for a segment to end, then for transcription and analysis.
Each segment is analysed on its own. Nothing carries over from earlier in the conversation apart from the end-of-session summary.
Speaker names are guessed from the transcript text, not identified from the audio.
Suggestions can be wrong. The model can misread a question or produce a plausible but unsuitable reply, which is why every draft is labelled as a suggestion and can be edited.
Not security-reviewed. It's built for local experimentation, not for handling other people's conversations at work.
nextSteps: Test with target users before adding features
Carry recent context between segments, as the design brief planned
Evaluate supported Microsoft Teams options, such as post-meeting transcripts, before any deeper integration
Add automated tests for the transcription and analysis path using fictional recorded fixtures
